opener.heading: Week 23: Colors of Summer ☀️
about: Color is the one thing Azlyn has all the words for, so this week takes it apart. She mixes red into five pinks a dot of white at a time, freezes color and drags it across paper, drops it onto wet paper and gets a circle every time, leaves it out in the sun until it fades, and pours it bowl to bowl until all three go brown. Every day she guesses first and looks second, and you write down both.

Kreston turns 1 on Saturday. Day 156 gives him a banana cake he is allowed to wreck, one candle for ten seconds, a walk down the block on one finger, a pencil line on the door frame, and the museum after lunch. Azlyn chooses his icing color at breakfast and then has to keep her hands off the cake, which is the hardest thing anyone does all week.
azlyn: Color is something you make. Red walks to pink in five steps, one dot of white at a time.
Guess first, look second. She calls what the cabbage water will do before the lemon goes in, and both answers go on the paper in the same pen.
Do it twice. The same red ice cube down a second sheet, to find out whether the world repeats itself when nobody changes anything.
Counting with a reason. Five blue and two red, dropped in with a teaspoon and spooned back out, gives her a color she can build again from her own card.
Things move without being touched. The sun pulling color out of paper over four hours, a balloon lifting paper it never reaches.
you: Appreciation is different from praise, and children need more of the first
Things that break the rules are the best teachers
Repeating an experiment is what makes it an experiment
"Why is it always round?" is a question worth leaving open
Same object, different result, and the variable is time
Being wrong in public is a skill, and it's built cheaply here
Invisible forces are a big conceptual step
shopping: Washable non-toxic poster paint in red, blue, yellow and white
Food coloring, a full set of bottles (four of the seven days use it)
Thick paper, 6 sheets, for the ice painting
Dark sugar paper, 3 sheets, or dark gift wrap
Colored paper, tissue paper and old magazine pages
Plain paper, a few sheets, for writing her guesses on
Index cards or cut card, 6, for the color recipes
A permanent marker and a pen
A pair of adult scissors (adult only)
Pencils, 3, two of them short and blunt
A paintbrush and a jar for the brush water
An old plate for a palette, and a white saucer
Plastic cups, 4, that can go outside
Teaspoons, 6 (a clean one per test on Wednesday)
Trays, 4: one metal, one with a lip, one shallow enough for Kreston to sit at
A mixing bowl, a spatula and a fork
Two spare bowls, one for the cabbage water and one for warm water
A small cake pan, a ramekin or an oven-safe mug
Plain yogurt, and cream cheese or thick yogurt for the icing
An old sheet or a shower curtain for the floor
Stones, a handful, to weight paper down
An empty crisp packet, rinsed and dried
Colored grocery bags, ribbon and crepe offcuts
A stick, or a fence post you can tie to
Your phone, with last June's photos findable on it
opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 11 months this week. He stands alone for a few seconds before he sits back down, and babbles in long strings at anyone who answers. He turns 1 on Saturday the 5th, and from that morning he is walking or close to it, drinking from a cup and following a one-step instruction.

days.title: The Color Ladder
days.prepTonight: Cut six strips of thick card from a cereal box, two fingers wide, and stand the paints and a jar of water beside them. Buy a ripe banana and a candle.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: Five Steps from Red to Pink

opening.title: White Changes Everything
opening.need: 1 old plate · red poster paint · white poster paint · 1 brush · 1 jar of water · 1 cloth.
steps: Put a blob of red on one side of the plate and let her look at it.
Add a dot of white beside it and hand her the brush. She stirs, and the red turns into something else.
Add more white and ask whether it is still red. Take her answer, and tell her five of these are waiting at 9:15.

main.title: Five Steps from Red to Pink
materials: 6 strips of thick card cut from a cereal box
Washable poster paint in red, blue and yellow
steps: Rule three of the strips into five boxes each with the marker. Put the other three strips to one side, blank.
Box one on the first strip gets red straight from the pot, no white at all.
Scrape a little red onto the plate, stir in a dot of white, and fill box two. More white for box three, more again for four and five, until the last box has almost no red left.
Rinse the brush in the jar, dry it on the cloth, and run the whole ladder again with blue, then with yellow.
Stand all three strips along the windowsill. Ask which two boxes are hardest to tell apart and let her hold the strip to the light.
Check the red strip with a finger at 10:15. It dries first, and it goes out with her.
main.tip: Add the white in doses smaller than feel worth doing. A big spoonful jumps her from red to pink and loses the three steps in between.

outside.title: What Matches the Card
paras: Take the dry red strip and a paper bag up the road. She hunts for anything matching a box on it: a brick, a car door, a geranium in a tub, a bottle cap. The street is at full color by June, so let the bag fill up.

days.infant: Kreston is 11 months and stands alone for a few seconds before he sits back down. Hand him a spare card strip in the stroller and let him chew the corner. Back at the table, sit him where he can watch the brush move.

second.title: The Summer Color Board
second.intro: The strips are dry by lunch and the bag has not been opened since the walk. This afternoon they meet on one big sheet.
materials: The paper bag from the walk
steps: Tip the bag out at one end of the table and let her spread everything flat.
Tape the three strips down the left edge of the big card, well apart, so there is room beside every box.
She takes one thing at a time, holds it against the strips, and finds its box. Her answer stands, even where you would have put it two along.
Glue or tape it beside that box. Petals go under tape rather than glue, because glue soaks them dark.
Trim the long stalks and anything too fat to lie flat. You cut, she holds.
Write beside each thing what it is, in marker, in her words. A pebble she calls a moon rock is a moon rock.
Title across the top: her name, June, and the year. Hang it at her eye height, which puts it above Kreston, because a taped-on bottle cap comes off in his hand.
second.tip: She will put something in a box you would swear is wrong. Leave it. Move it and the board becomes yours and she stops sorting.

alternatives: Sort the walk treasure into piles by color and stop there.
Tape the strips to the window and hold things up behind them.
Paint a fourth strip in greens for the garden.
Glue the whole bagful onto one sheet in no order.
outAgain: Playgroup, and the color board comes off the wall and goes under your arm to show whoever is there
The park, for the flowerbeds by the gate
The road with the most front yards
The corner store, and she chooses a drink by its color
The green space with a ball, if the board overran

aroundWorld.title: Colors Mean Different Things 🎨
paras: Color carries a different message depending on where you stand. Across much of East Asia white belongs to mourning and funerals, while red belongs to weddings, luck and money. Languages divide color up in their own ways too: Russian keeps separate basic words for light and dark blue, the way English keeps red and pink apart, and the Japanese word ao covers a stretch English splits between blue and green.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Cook plain rice for dinner and stir a pinch of turmeric through half of it. Yellow rice sits on celebration tables from Spain to South Asia. Put both bowls out and let Azlyn choose.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: The go light on a Japanese traffic signal is called blue.

days.krestonPM: He gets a square of card of his own and one thing out of the bag too big to swallow: a leaf the size of your hand, a pebble he cannot close a fist around. At 11 months he passes objects hand to hand. Sit him near the table, where he can pull up on a chair leg.

insight.headline: Appreciation is different from praise, and children need more of the first.
paras: Good job lands on Azlyn as a verdict. She hears that you approved, has no idea which part, and the next strip is aimed at collecting the verdict again. Appreciation hands her the detail back: you mixed white in five times before you stopped, or there are three reds here and this morning I could see one. Children given descriptive feedback stay with hard work longer and hold up better when it goes wrong, because their read on it sits in the work rather than your face. Thank her for the board on the wall too, which appreciates her rather than the paint.

days.safety: Kreston is 11 months and mouths everything he can reach. Walk treasure is small: bottle caps, pebbles, petals, a feather. It goes back in the paper bag and up out of his reach the second you stop watching him, and the finished board hangs at her eye height, above his reach, for the same reason. Washable non-toxic paint only. The scissors stay with you.

days.title: Kreston Is One
days.prepTonight: Leave a spotty banana on the side and find last June's photos tonight. Check you have two ice-cube trays and craft sticks for tomorrow.

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: Everywhere He Can Get To Now

opening.title: Choosing Kreston's Color
opening.need: the food coloring bottles · 1 white saucer · 1 teaspoon.
steps: Line the bottles up at breakfast and put one drop of each on the saucer, well apart.
Half a teaspoon of water onto each drop, and she stirs them open with the spoon handle.
Tell her Kreston's cake gets one of them and she chooses. She will change her mind twice, so take the last answer.

main.title: The Smash Cake
materials: 1 small pan, ramekin or oven-safe mug
steps: She mashes the banana in the bowl with the fork until she cannot find a lump.
Egg in, yogurt in, and she beats the lot with the same fork. Lumps are fine.
Four tablespoons of flour, counted in by her and folded through with the spatula.
Scrape it into the pan and bake it at 350°F for twenty-five minutes. You open the door and you carry the pan, both times.
Turn it out onto the tray and stand it somewhere cold. Cream cheese slides off a warm cake, so it has until one o'clock. Washing the bowl is her job while it cools.
main.tip: Build it for wrecking. Anything you tidy up turns it into a cake somebody wants kept, and this one has about eleven minutes to live.

outside.title: Everywhere He Can Get To Now
paras: Walk the block and stop at four places Kreston could do nothing with last June: the low wall, the front step, the slope to the gate, the rough patch where the sidewalk lifts. Set him down at each with a finger to hold, and send Azlyn ahead to show him. She announces every success first.

days.infant: Kreston turns 1 today. Say the birthday out loud to his face, because nobody else will. Twelve months is where the walking starts arriving in earnest, so set him down on the flat outside and hold one finger rather than two. He drinks from an open cup with your hand under it, and he follows a one-step instruction now, so hand him a wooden spoon and say bang. Give him the empty yogurt pot while Azlyn mashes and mixes, then put him in the high chair before the pan goes in the oven and leave him there until it is back out and the door is shut.

second.title: One Candle, One Year
second.intro: A sheet on the floor, a cake on the sheet, and a one-year-old who has never been told he is allowed to destroy something.
materials: The cold cake from this morning
4 tbsp cream cheese or thick yogurt, and food coloring in the shade she chose
1 small bowl and 1 spoon for the icing
1 lighter or a box of matches (adult only)
3 balloons, inflated by you, kept above head height between goes
1 old sheet or shower curtain for the floor
1 wet washcloth in a shallow bowl
Your phone, and last June's photos
steps: Cream cheese into the small bowl, two drops of the color she picked, and she stirs the streaks out. She spreads it over the cold cake and pushes the candle into the middle. No neatening from you.
Blow the balloons up yourself and let Azlyn bat them round while you spread the sheet.

Cake in the middle, Kreston in front of it, everyone else on the floor at his level. Light the candle, sing, blow it out yourself after ten seconds, then lift the candle out of the cake and put it up high before his hands go anywhere near it.
Hands off him. He goes in with one finger, then a fist, then his face. Azlyn will want to help, and the answer is no.
Washcloth over his face and hands at the end, rinsed in the bowl between passes.
Hand Azlyn your phone and let her film a minute of him with the icing still on his chin, saying his name and his age into it.
Both of them at the door frame, mark with the pencil, date and name each line. Then bring up last June's photos and hold the phone against the wall.
second.tip: Some babies hate it. Kreston may stare at the cake or object to the texture. Push one finger in for him, then leave him be.

alternatives: Wall marks and the minute of film only, and skip the cake.
One candle in a bowl of yogurt, sung over, and out.
Photograph his hands, his feet and his teeth up close.
Let Azlyn open his presents, which is what she wants.
outAgain: The museum, first Saturday of June and his birthday outing
The farm, if the museum is booked out
Grandparents, or whoever wants to see him today
The garden and the kiddie pool, if the morning was enough
days.krestonPM: A museum is loud, so give it forty minutes and leave before he tells you to. At twelve months he would rather walk than look, so find an empty stretch of floor and let him do laps holding one of your fingers. Azlyn picks the room.

insight.headline: Things that break the rules are the best teachers.
paras: Kreston has spent a year learning that food stays in a bowl, hands get wiped and cake belongs on a plate. This afternoon all three come off at once and his face does the work. Babies look longer at events that break what they expected, and afterwards they investigate the object that misbehaved rather than the one that behaved. A ball that hangs in the air gets shaken. A cake he may sit in gets taken apart with both hands. Azlyn gets the same gift from the other side, watching a rule suspended on purpose and learning that rules have edges.

days.safety: The oven is on for half an hour this morning, so say it out loud when Azlyn comes near, and Kreston is in the high chair or out of the kitchen while the pan goes in and comes out. Balloons are the other one. Uninflated and burst latex is among the worst choking hazards there is under three, so you inflate them, they stay above head height, and a burst balloon is picked up whole and thrown out before Kreston is back down. The candle is lit for ten seconds, blown out by an adult, then out of the cake and up high. No honey for Kreston, no whole grapes, no whole nuts.

days.title: The Colors That Melt
days.prepTonight: Fill two ice-cube trays with water, stir a different food coloring into each row, stand a craft stick in every cube once they are half set, and freeze them overnight.

opening.title: Cracking Out the Cubes
opening.need: the two frozen trays · 1 metal baking tray · 1 old towel.
steps: Twist each tray over the metal one and let her push the cubes out from underneath. A few snap off their sticks, and the broken ones still work, so they stay on the tray.
Sort them into color piles on the tray and count each pile out loud.
Stand the tray on the table out of Kreston's reach, drop the towel by the back door and go and find your shoes. They are melting already.

main.title: Ice Painting on the Path
materials: 2 trays of colored ice cubes frozen overnight with craft sticks in them, or plain cubes from the freezer door with a drop of coloring dripped beside each one on the paper
1 bowl of warm water for cold hands
steps: Chalk a straight line across the paving and lay two sheets of paper with their top edges against it.
She takes a red cube by the stick and drags it from the line down the paper. It goes on pale, then floods behind itself.
Fresh sheet, same red, same line, same direction. Ask her first whether it will do the same thing twice.
Run all three colors twice, one sheet each, and leave the pairs side by side on the path.
Let her draw onto the paving with a cube and watch the sun take the line back inside a few minutes.
Hands into the bowl of warm water when they go red, then dried on the towel. Spare cubes stay up on the metal tray between runs.
main.tip: She will press harder to get it darker. Let her, then run one with no pressure at all. Melt does more of this than muscle.

outside.title: Every Green on One Street
paras: Walk one street and count greens. One road in June holds more of them than the rest of the year puts together: new leaf on the hedge, dark holly, the blue-green of a spruce, grass, moss in the wall, a trash can, somebody's front door. Ask her for two greens that are not the same green, then hold the leaf against the trash can lid.

days.infant: Kreston is 12 months and copies a job he has watched somebody else do. Hand him a corner of the old towel and say wipe. Keep him off the wet paving and away from the ice. Sit him in sight of the drying paper, out of reach of it.

second.title: Five Blue, Two Red
second.intro: Everything in this one gets counted, and a color she invents gets built twice.
materials: 6 cards and 1 pen for the recipes
steps: Paper towels down first, tray on top, six cups on the tray, each half full of water from the tap.
She invents the first color. Drops go in one at a time and she counts them out loud: five blue, two red.
Write the numbers on a card while she watches. Whatever she calls the color goes on the card too.
Second cup, and she builds it again from her own card. You read the numbers back and she counts the drops in.
Hold the two cups to the window side by side. If they do not match, count what went in and hunt for the missing drop.
If one comes out too strong, she spoons some off with the teaspoon and tops the cup back up with water.
Three recipes is plenty, and that is your six cups. Lay the cards along the table with their cups behind them and photograph the row.
second.tip: Let her name them. Dragon and sad blue and Kreston beat dark purple, because a name she invented is one she can find again a week later.

alternatives: Two cups and one recipe, then stop.
Mix the colors in an ice tray instead and freeze them for tomorrow.
Paint with the leftover colored water and a brush.
Line the six cups up from lightest to darkest.
outAgain: The nature hunt walk, with a bag and one rule: nothing green
The woods, for the cool under the trees
The park, and a lap of the flowerbeds
The duck pond, if the afternoon has gone loud
The garden with the hose
days.krestonPM: Give him a cup of his own on the tray with two centimeters of water in it and no coloring. At twelve months he tips, pours and puts a whole hand in, and he will drink out of it, which is why his is clear. Paper towels underneath him and a change of top on the chair.

insight.headline: Repeating an experiment is what makes it an experiment.
paras: Running the red cube twice looks like an afternoon of the same thing. Azlyn is doing what every scientist does before a result counts, checking that the world behaves the same way when nobody changed anything. A three-year-old has no reason to assume it will. Her days are full of one-offs, and the idea that a cause repeats gets built out of cases she watched happen twice. The second run is also the only thing she can compare the first against, so it is where small differences show up. Say the numbers out loud both times and let her call the match.

days.safety: Colored ice cubes look like something to eat, and a cube is the wrong size and shape for a one-year-old. Keep the metal tray up on the kitchen table, count them out and count them back. Craft sticks stay off the floor. Wet paving is slippery under bare feet, so shoes on for the painting.

days.title: Everything Comes Out Round
days.prepTonight: Stand the paper towels, the coffee filters and the food coloring on the baking tray. If you have no dark paper for Tuesday, paint a flattened cereal box black so it dries overnight.

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: The Round Light Under the Tree

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Books on the Bed, Nothing Else

opening.title: One Drop at a Time
opening.need: 1 sheet of paper towels · 1 cup of water with three drops of color stirred in · 1 teaspoon.
steps: Lay the sheet flat on the table and let her load the spoon out of the cup.
One drop, from a hand's height. Then both of you stop and count to ten while it opens.
Ask what shape it made. Do three more in the corners before she can decide the first was a fluke.

main.title: Every Drop Makes a Circle
materials: Food coloring in 3 cups, each half filled with water
steps: A sheet of paper towels flat in the tray. Damp it from the pitcher and press it down with her palm.
One drop from as high as she can reach. It lands wide and opens fast.
One drop from a finger's width above the paper, spoon almost touching. Round again, and smaller.
Fresh dry sheet, and the same two drops onto it. The circle on dry paper takes its time and comes out with a harder edge.
Open a coffee filter flat and put two colors down close enough that the circles run into one another.
Last filter, no rules: as many drops as she wants until there is no white left on it.
main.tip: Do not answer why it comes out round. Ask her instead, take whatever she says, and leave the question open for the rest of the week.

outside.title: The Round Light Under the Tree
paras: Stand under the leafiest tree on the street on a bright June morning and look down. The light through the gaps lands in dozens of small discs, and every one is round even though not one gap up there is. Hold paper underneath so she can see the edges, then move it up and down and watch them grow.

days.infant: Kreston is 12 months and picks the smallest thing off the floor with a finger and thumb. Give him a dry coffee filter to crumple, open and crumple again, and take it back before it goes in his mouth. Under the tree, lay him on his back.

second.title: Spinning the Colors Away
second.intro: A disc of card, a pencil through the middle, and colors she can make vanish by turning them fast enough.
materials: 1 hard flat tray to spin on
steps: She draws round the cup on the flattened card six times, and you cut the discs out.
The first disc is hers to color however she likes. Markers go on stronger than crayons and spin better for it.
Push the scissor point through the center to start a hole, then work a short pencil through so the disc sits low, near the point.
Spin it on the tray with two fingers and let her watch her colors go gray.
Second disc, two colors only, one on each half. Spin that and see what blue and yellow give you.
Put the other pencil through a third disc so two can run at once and she can race them.
Leave three blank discs and the markers out on the table for later.
second.tip: A disc riding high on the pencil wobbles and drops. Push it down to within a finger's width of the point and it will run for ten seconds at a time.

alternatives: Color the discs and skip the spinning.
Spin them on a smooth floor instead of the tray.
Draw one thick spiral on a disc and spin that.
Tape a disc into the salad spinner and turn the handle.
outAgain: The duck pond, and count the greens on one drake's head
The riverside path, for the shade along it
The park, if the sprinkler is on
A friend's garden, and take two spare discs
The green space with a ball
days.krestonPM: He gets a blank disc, wider than his mouth, with nothing sharp in it and no pencil through it. At twelve months he bangs two things together and waits for the noise, so hand him two. At the pond keep him on the grass side of the path and let him practice standing up out of a squat.

insight.headline: "Why is it always round?" is a question worth leaving open.
paras: Azlyn asked, you have an answer about surface tension, and she is three. Handing it over closes the file. A question she carries for a week does more work than a fact she takes at nine in the morning, because she keeps testing it: on the filter, under the tree, in the bath tonight. Hand the question back (what do you think, shall we try it) and she asks more of them, and the asking outlives every answer you have. Say I do not know out loud, and often. She finds out that adults live with open questions, and that carrying one around is survivable.

days.safety: The scissors are adult-only and Kreston is one and on his feet. Cut the discs while he is in the high chair, and put the scissors back on a shelf between cuts rather than on the arm of the chair. The short pencils are mouth-sized, so they come off the floor before he goes down. A disc drawn round the cup is wider than his mouth, so one blank disc is his and nothing with a pencil through it.

days.title: The Sun Takes the Color
days.prepTonight: Check the dark sheets are dry and stand them by the back door with a handful of stones. Pack the swim bags, and buy a red cabbage while you are out today.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Paper Left in the Sun

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: Things the Sun Got To First

opening.title: Picking the Flat Things
opening.need: 1 tray or basket · one of the dark sheets · her, going round the house.
steps: Walk her round the house hunting for six things that lie flat. Keys, a fork, a comb, a craft stick, two leaves off the garden.
Test each on the dark sheet, looking sideways for a gap of light underneath. Anything that rocks goes back.
Load the six into the tray and carry it out. She picks the sunniest spot and her choice stands.

main.title: The Paper Left in the Sun
materials: 2 sheets of dark sugar paper (a flattened cereal box painted dark works, or dark gift wrap)
6 flat objects: keys, a fork, leaves, a comb, a craft stick, and a paper shape she cuts
1 scrap of paper for her to cut
Stones or clothespins to weight the edges
Your phone, for the before photo
steps: She cuts a shape out of a paper scrap with the child scissors. Whatever comes out is the sixth object.
Lay one dark sheet flat in the spot she chose and let her arrange all six on it, spaced so nothing overlaps.
Weight the corners with stones, and lay a clothespin along any edge that lifts.
Write the time in marker on the corner of the sheet and photograph it from above.
The second sheet goes indoors on a shelf away from every window, bare, same time on it. That one is the comparison.
Leave both until 1:00, and agree now that the looking happens after lunch.
main.tip: Choose the spot for where the sun will be at noon, not nine thirty. A sheet in shade by eleven gives you nothing to hold up later.

outside.title: Things the Sun Got To First
paras: Walk the street hunting for what the sun has already bleached. A red slide gone pink, a for-sale sign faded pale in a window, dry yellow grass on the sunny strip by the curb and green grass in the shade of the wall. Ask her which side of the street the sun works on hardest. Then find one color twice, once out in the light and once in the shade, and hold the two of them together. Your hand goes flat on any dark paint before hers does.

days.infant: Kreston is 12 months and this is his first real June sun on his own feet. Hat, shade and sunscreen before he goes out. He will make straight for the stones, so keep the sheet at the far end of the garden and give him a big cup and a folded washcloth in the shade, nothing smaller. At a year he moves things between containers twenty times over.

second.title: What the Sun Left Behind
second.intro: Nothing has happened out there for four hours. Go and look anyway.
materials: The sun sheet and the indoor sheet
1 large sheet of card to mount it on
1 fresh sheet of dark paper, and six new objects
steps: Go out together and take the stones off first. She lifts each object herself, and you both stop after the first to look.
Carry both sheets in and lay the indoor one on top of the sun sheet, edge to edge.
Slide them apart a hand's width. The difference reads best at the seam.
Glue the sun sheet onto the big card and tape the indoor sheet beside it.
Write both times on the card in marker, and underneath, what she says in her own words.
Set the next one running: fresh dark sheet in the same spot, six new objects she picks, stones on the corners, time written on.
Look again after dinner and see whether the afternoon sheet got as far as the morning one.
second.tip: The prints go on fading indoors. Photograph the card today, because by Friday the shapes will have caught up with the rest of the sheet.

alternatives: Lift the objects, look, and put them straight back for another hour.
Do the same with a dish towel on the clothesline.
Draw round the six objects instead of mounting the print.
Start a sheet somewhere shady and compare the two tomorrow.
outAgain: Swimming, and the coldest thing anyone touches today
The kiddie pool at home if the session is full
A splash pad or a fountain
The park and a picnic in the shade
The garden and the hose, if nobody can face the changing rooms
days.krestonPM: He comes into the pool with you. At twelve months he walks on land and has no notion that it stops working in water, so he is in your hands from the changing room to the car. Walk him along the wall under the arms and let him pat it. Twenty minutes, and out before his lips go.

insight.headline: Same object, different result, and the variable is time.
paras: Two sheets of the same paper, and one of them changed. Azlyn can see the difference at the seam, and she cannot see the thing that caused it, because the cause was four hours going by. Time as a cause is hard at three. Her working model of why anything happens runs on contact: you push it, it moves. Something that changes while nobody touched it needs another sort of explanation, and she builds that out of days like this one, where the only difference between two sheets is how long each sat there. The indoor sheet argues it for you.

days.safety: June sun. Hat, shade and sunscreen before 10:30, and put your own hand flat on the paving before she goes out barefoot. Dark paper, stones and a dark car hood all hold heat well past what her hands and feet will take, so you test each one first. At the pool, Kreston is one and within arm's reach in the water, every second, no exceptions.

days.title: Purple Cabbage Water
days.prepTonight: Chop half a red cabbage, cover it with boiling water in a bowl and leave it overnight. It goes deep purple by morning, and the smell is the price of admission.

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Library Books on the Floor

opening.title: Straining the Purple Water
opening.need: the bowl of cabbage water · 1 sieve · 1 pitcher.
steps: Hold the sieve over the pitcher and let her pour the bowl through it. The cabbage stays behind, the color goes through.
Hold the pitcher against the window. It reads purple in the light and near black on the table.
Stand the pitcher at her place and tell her this water changes color six times before lunch. Do not say how.

main.title: The Water That Turns Pink
materials: Red cabbage water, half a cabbage steeped overnight and strained, or the chopped cabbage simmered for ten minutes this morning and cooled in a bowl of cold water
steps: Six cups on the tray, each a third full of the strained cabbage water. Cup one gets nothing all morning and stays where she can see it.
Before anything goes in, hold up the lemon juice and ask what color it will make. Write her guess down in her words.
Two teaspoons of lemon juice into cup two. Write what happened beside the guess and read her both.
Same for the vinegar, then a teaspoon of baking soda, a squirt of dish soap, then sparkling water. Guess first every time, clean teaspoon each time.
Pour the pink cup into the green cup and let her call what is coming before it lands.
Line all six along the windowsill beside cup one and read the guesses back from the top.
main.tip: Write the wrong guesses in the same hand as the right ones. She will notice if you skip one, and a sheet of only hits is worth nothing to her.

outside.title: Six Purple Things
paras: June is the purple month around here and she needs six. Lavender by a front step, allium heads gone to seed, clover in the grass, a sticker on a bin, somebody's front door, a hydrangea gone bruise-purple by a porch. Photograph each so all six come home, ask which is closest to the pitcher on the kitchen table, and let her argue for one you would not have picked.

days.infant: Kreston is 12 months and points at what he wants. Walk at half speed for ten minutes and follow his finger, naming whatever it lands on. Indoors, keep him well back from the cups, because cabbage water looks like grape juice. Give him plain water on his tray and let him tip it over.

second.title: Pouring Color into Color
second.intro: Three bowls on the grass and nothing small to be careful with, after a morning working in teaspoons.
materials: 1 shallow tray with 2 cm of water for Kreston
steps: Three bowls out on the grass, well apart, filled from the tap with the pitchers. She carries them out one at a time.
Color each bowl a color of its own, one bottle per bowl, and she does the squeezing.
Give her the cups and let her pour red into blue until the whole bowlful turns.
Funnel into a cup next, then funnel into a bowl, then funnel over her own foot.
Hand her the sieve and say nothing. She will try to carry water in it three or four times.
Kreston's shallow tray goes on a towel at the far end, two centimeters of clear water, his alone.
Tip every bowl out onto the grass before anyone goes in, and bring the towels with you.
second.tip: All three bowls go muddy inside twenty minutes and nothing can be done about it. Treat that as the finish. Let her pour the lot into one brown bowl and tip it out herself.

alternatives: One bowl, one pitcher, and a color that changes once.
Fill the bowls and leave the coloring out of it.
Wash the dolls in the colored water.
Paint the fence with a brush and a bowl of plain water.
outAgain: The library, the every two weeks one, and she picks a book by its cover color
Indoor playground, if the library session is packed out
The park on the way home
A café, and the new books read once through
The duck pond, for the shade under the willow
days.krestonPM: At the library he goes in the board-book corner and chews what he finds. At twelve months he carries a book over and drops it in your lap, and that is a request. Read it three times. Azlyn chooses his and carries it to the desk.

insight.headline: Being wrong in public is a skill, and it's built cheaply here.
paras: Azlyn said green, the cup went pink, and you wrote both down in the same pen. Nothing bad happened to her. Cabbage water is the cheapest place she will ever be wrong, and that cost is what she is learning this morning, well ahead of the chemistry. A prediction that gets written down and then checked, by somebody who stays flat about the outcome, is one she will make out loud again. Corrected often enough, she goes quiet and waits to be told instead. Read the wrong guesses back in the voice you use for the right ones, and she will still be guessing at eleven, when it counts for more.

days.safety: Standing water and a one-year-old on his feet. A dishwashing bowl is deep enough to drown in, so you stay outside for the whole of it and every bowl gets tipped out before anyone goes in. Baking soda and vinegar sting eyes, so no rubbing with wet hands, and keep the cups back from the table edge. Cabbage water stains clothes and grout.

days.title: Colors That Move on Their Own
days.prepTonight: Stack colored paper, tissue and old magazine pages on the table with the metal tray, and dig the wool sweater out of the closet.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: The Smallest Pieces She Can Tear

opening.title: The Smallest Pieces She Can Tear
opening.need: colored paper, tissue and magazine pages · 1 metal tray.
steps: Fingers only this morning. No scissors, and say so at the start so she stops asking.
She tears, then tears the pieces again, then again. Ask for pieces smaller than her thumbnail and let her go past where you would have stopped.
Spread the lot in a thin layer across the metal tray and leave it. Something happens to it at 9:15.

main.title: The Colors That Jump
materials: 2 balloons, inflated by an adult, kept above head height when nobody is holding one
1 empty crisp packet, rinsed and dried
steps: Spread the torn paper across the tray and hold a balloon a hand's width above it. Nothing moves.
Rub the same balloon on her hair, twenty strokes, counted out by her.
Hold it back over the tray at the same height. The paper comes up off the metal to meet it.
Rub a second balloon on the wool sweater and run the same test. She calls which lifted more before either of you looks.
Go hunting. Balloon behind her head and her hair follows. Balloon beside a thin stream from the kitchen tap and the water bends over. Balloon near the crisp packet and it slides.
Let her find one more thing in the house that moves. She will try twenty and land one.
main.tip: It fails on a humid day. If nothing lifts, take it to the carpet in a warm room with the window shut and rub for longer than feels sensible.

outside.title: The Ribbon Test
paras: Take one length of ribbon out and hold it up in six places: the front step, the corner, the open end of the street, behind the hedge, under the trees, out in the middle of the green. It hangs dead in some spots and streams in others. Let her call the windiest before you get there.

days.infant: Kreston is 12 months and he cannot have the balloons, so give him the wool sweater on the floor and let him haul it about. At a year he pulls, drags and carries things while he walks. Outside, hand him one end of the ribbon and keep hold of the other.

second.title: Ribbons Where the Wind Is
second.intro: The wind has been doing all the work out there for a week without her seeing any of it. A line of strips fixes that in four minutes.
materials: 2 m of string, or the clothesline
Colored grocery bags, ribbon and crepe offcuts
steps: Cut the grocery bags into long strips a hand's width across. You cut, she says how long each gets to be.
Tie the string high between the fence post and the stick pushed into the border, above the reach of anyone small. Or clip the strips to the clothesline and leave the string in the drawer.
She clips the strips along it, spaced out, in whatever order she likes.
Both of you stand back. They all point the same way, and that way is the wind.
Draw an arrow on the fence post with the marker showing where they point, and write the time beside it.
Move one strip to the stillest corner she found this morning and compare it against the line.
Check the arrow after dinner. It will have moved or it will not.
second.tip: Tie it high and step back. Half of this is standing still looking at something you set up, and she does that for as long as you do it first.

alternatives: One ribbon tied to the gate and nothing else.
Bubbles, and watch which way they go.
A carrier-bag kite on a short string, run down the garden.
Hang the strips in the doorway indoors and open a window.
outAgain: The bakery run, and she chooses by color: the pink one, the brown one, the yellow one
The corner store for milk, and she carries it home
The park on the way back
A bench, the paper bag, and one thing each
The long way home, past the gardens
days.krestonPM: He walks the last hundred yards holding one of your fingers, which at twelve months takes as long as you let it take. Give him a crust to hold in the bakery. Back home he gets the empty paper bag. At a year old it holds him longer than whatever came in it.

insight.headline: Invisible forces are a big conceptual step.
paras: Everything Azlyn has worked out about why things move runs through contact. A hand pushes, a foot kicks, wind arrives on her face. A balloon that lifts paper without touching it breaks that rule, and the real answer sits years past three. She can take the pattern today: something happened here, and the cause was not touching. She meets the idea again in magnets, in the sun that faded her paper on Tuesday, and one day in gravity. Give her the word and leave the mechanism alone. Naming a thing she cannot see is the first handhold on it, and the explanation keeps for a few years.

days.safety: Balloons again. You inflate them, nobody hands Kreston one, they stay above head height between goes, and a burst balloon is picked up whole and thrown out before he is back on the floor. Uninflated and burst latex is among the worst choking hazards there is for a child under three. The string and the ribbon go up out of reach the moment you finish, and the wind line is tied high on the fence, never at his height. The scissors stay with you.
